questions.q: What is serialization?
questions.explain: A value must become text or bytes before it goes into a queue, a cache, a file or an HTTP response. Turning the text back into a value is deserialization. Checking the shape is validation, a separate step.
options: Turning a value in memory into text or bytes, so it can leave the process
Checking that a value has the right shape
Encrypting a value before it is stored
Running functions one after another, in order

questions.q: Which value can plain JSON hold without changing it?
questions.explain: JSON only knows strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays and plain objects. A Date becomes a string, a Set becomes {}, and a BigInt is refused.
options: An array of strings and numbers

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify writes a Date as an ISO string, and JSON.parse has no way to know it was a date. Code that later calls back.due.getTime() crashes.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A Set and a Map keep their items in a hidden place, not in normal properties, so JSON sees empty objects. The tags and notes are silently gone, with no error.
options: TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a Set

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An error's message is not a normal enumerable property, so plain JSON writes {}. The message is lost.
questions.code:
const failure = { lastError: new Error("mail server is down") };
console.log(JSON.stringify(failure));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON refuses a BigInt with a TypeError. It will not guess, because a normal JSON number cannot hold that many digits exactly.

questions.q: A job's type says { remindAt: Date }, but after the queue the processor receives a string. Why does TypeScript not warn you?
questions.explain: TypeScript trusts the type you wrote. JSON turned the date into a string at runtime, and the program runs until the first line that uses it as a Date, such as remindAt.toISOString().
options: The queue turns off type checking
Types only exist when you compile; at runtime the data came from text, and nothing checked it
TypeScript does warn, but only in strict mode
Strings and dates are the same type in TypeScript

questions.q: npm says "up to date" when you install @zudojs/serialization, because the queue and cache already use it. Why install it yourself anyway?
questions.explain: If you import a package, list it. Otherwise a future version of the queue could drop or change that dependency, and your code breaks without any change of yours.
options: It is not needed; imports work through the other packages
It adds it to your package.json, so your code does not depend on another package's choices
It makes the package run faster
npm refuses imports that are not listed

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With preserveTypes: true, a value that JSON cannot hold becomes a small object with a $type tag and a $value. It is still valid JSON, and the reader can rebuild a real Date.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The tags let the reader rebuild each value: a real Date, a real Set and a real bigint. Plain JSON.parse would give a string, an empty object, and an error for the BigInt.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A BigInt is written as its digits in a string, so no precision is lost. A Set is written as an array of its items. Both carry a $type tag.
options: TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt

questions.q: How does the serializer write a Uint8Array of raw bytes?
questions.explain: Base64 is a compact way to write bytes as text. The tag says it was a byte array, so the reader rebuilds a real Uint8Array. Plain JSON would write { "0": 137, "1": 80, … }.
options: As an object with one key per byte
As a tagged value whose $value is base64: bytes written as plain letters
As a string of numbers separated by commas

questions.q: Where should you use preserveTypes: true?
questions.explain: The text is longer, and a service not written in JavaScript sees $type tags it does not know. For a public API, send plain JSON with dates as ISO strings, and parse them with a schema.
options: Where both sides are your own code, such as your queue and your cache
Nowhere; it is only for tests

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An error keeps its name and message. The stack trace is left out unless you ask for it with includeStack: true.
options: {"lastError":{"$type":"Error","name":"Error","message":"mail server is down","stack":"Error: mail server is down"}}

questions.q: Why does the serializer leave out an error's stack trace by default?
questions.explain: A stack trace lists your file names and code lines. Leaving it out is the safe default. Turn it on with includeStack: true only where you control who reads the data.
options: Stack traces are too long to fit in JSON
Serialized errors end up in queues and logs, and a stack trace tells an attacker about your code
Stack traces cannot be turned into strings
It is a bug that will be fixed

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A value that contains itself has no end, so it cannot be written out. The serializer stops with a clear CircularReferenceError, which also says where the loop is (root.parent).

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An invalid date is refused instead of being written as null (which is what plain JSON does). You find the bug where it happens, not later when a reminder never fires.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The text is about 2000 bytes, over the maxSize of 1000, so it is refused before it is parsed. That protects the program from huge payloads.

questions.q: Text arrives from another service. Which options should you set when you deserialize it?
questions.explain: Huge or very deeply nested text can use up memory or crash the reader. Set both limits whenever the text comes from outside.
options: None; the defaults trust all input
maxSize and maxDepth, to limit how big and how deeply nested it may be

questions.q: An attacker sends this text. What does this print?
questions.explain: The serializer drops __proto__, constructor and prototype keys while it rebuilds objects. So the user does not become an admin, and no other object in the program is changed either.

questions.q: A user's data happens to contain a $type key. What does this print?
questions.explain: A plain object that has a $type key is written inside an "Object" wrapper, and read back as the plain object it was. Your data can never pretend to be a tag.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: By default, a tag that makes no sense is left as plain data, so one bad record does not stop your consumer. With strict: true it throws instead.

questions.q: When should a queue consumer deserialize with strict: true?
questions.explain: Strict mode turns a broken tag into an error. In a queue, that error fails the job, and after its retries it lands in the dead letters where you can inspect it, instead of flowing on as half-broken data.
options: Never; it makes the consumer crash
When a bad payload should be rejected, for example so the job goes to the dead-letter queue

questions.q: A reminder with taskId: -5 deserializes without any error. What is missing?
questions.explain: The serializer only checks that the text is safe to rebuild. It does not know your app's rules. A schema checks that taskId is a positive whole number.
options: Nothing; the serializer already checked it
Validating the result with a schema, as with any outside input

questions.q: In a custom transformer for a Duration class, what must serialize return?
questions.explain: Without the $type tag, the reader cannot know the value was a Duration, and it comes back as a plain number.

questions.q: Why should a transformer's deserialize check its input before it builds the object?
questions.explain: deserialize is where outside text becomes your object. Throw on bad input, such as $value: -5, instead of creating a broken Duration.
options: It receives data from outside, which may be missing or wrong, like a negative number of minutes
It does not need to; the serializer checks it

questions.q: How do you add your own Duration type and keep the built-in Date, Map and Set support?
questions.explain: registerTransformer adds your type next to the built-in ones, which is why the date in the lesson's example still works.
options: Change the $type of every Date to "Duration"

questions.q: What does an envelope add to serialized text?
questions.explain: Like the address and stamp on a letter, the envelope tells the reader how to read the data. The reader checks it first and refuses a format or version it does not understand.
options: Metadata the reader needs: the format, the version of that format, the content type and encoding
A signature that proves who sent it

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The metadata says the format is json, version 1 of the tagging format. data is the serialized text, not the object.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The reader asked for messagepack, but the envelope says json. It is refused with a clear error instead of being misread.
options: Unsupported envelope schema version 1: this build understands up to 1

questions.q: What does the envelope's version describe?
questions.explain: The envelope version belongs to the serializer. For changes to your data, put your own v field in the payload.
options: The version of your reminder payload
The serializer's tagging format, not your data
How many times the value was serialized

questions.q: Why put a v field in every payload from day one?
questions.explain: With v: 1 in every payload, the reader always knows which shape it holds and can upgrade it step by step.
options: The queue refuses payloads without it
Adding it later means guessing what a payload without one is

questions.q: You change the reminder job from version 1 to version 2. In which order do you deploy?
questions.explain: If writers go first, old readers receive version 2 payloads they cannot read. Readers first means every payload that exists can always be read.
options: Readers first: ship code that can read version 2, then code that writes it
Both at once, and empty the queue

questions.q: You add a new optional field to a payload. Do you need a new version?
questions.explain: Only adding where you can keeps changes painless. A new version is needed when you remove or rename a field, or change its meaning.
options: Yes, every change needs a new version
No: old readers ignore it, and new readers use a default when it is missing
Yes, or the envelope refuses it
No, but you must empty the queue first

questions.q: When can you delete the code that upgrades version 1 payloads?
questions.explain: Stored payloads outlive deploys. As long as a version 1 job may still sit in the queue, the reader must understand it.
options: When no version 1 payload can exist any more: the queue is empty of them and cache entries have expired

questions.q: How does the lesson make the reminder queue keep its Date?
questions.explain: The queue serializes every job's data. Giving it a serializer with preserveTypes: true tags the date on the way in and rebuilds a real Date for the processor.
options: Convert every date to a string by hand before add
Use JSON.stringify with a replacer in the processor
Store the dates in a global Map

questions.q: Types are kept at any depth. What does this print?
questions.explain: The date inside the Map was tagged too, so it comes back as a real Date. toISOString() always prints milliseconds: .000Z.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A version 1 payload is upgraded on read. When the upgrade cannot work (no user for that email) it throws, instead of creating a version 2 payload with userId: undefined.
options:
{ v: 2, taskId: 1, userId: 'user-ada' }
No user for bob@example.com

{ v: 1, taskId: 1, email: 'ada@example.com' }
No user for bob@example.com

{ v: 2, taskId: 1, userId: 'user-ada' }
{ v: 2, taskId: 2, userId: undefined }

questions.q: Finish lostKeys(value): send value through plain JSON.stringify and JSON.parse, and return the keys whose value changed its typeof or its constructor name (for objects). The program should print [ 'due', 'tags' ].
questions.explain: After the round trip, due is a string (it was a Date) and tags is a plain Object (it was a Set). id and title survive. This is why a typed serializer is needed.

questions.q: Finish roundTrip(value) so it serializes and deserializes value with a serializer from @zudojs/serialization that keeps types. The program should print true 2 true.
questions.explain: createSerializer("json", { preserveTypes: true }) tags the Date, Set and BigInt on the way out and rebuilds them on the way back. Without the option you would get a string, an empty object and an error.

questions.q: Messages arrive from another service. Finish readMessage(text): deserialize with a limit of 200 bytes (maxSize) and strict: true. Return the value, or the string "rejected: " followed by the error's name if it throws. The program should print the three lines in the comments.
questions.explain: Pass the options as the second argument of deserialize. maxSize refuses oversized text before it is parsed, and strict turns a broken tag into an error you can reject.

questions.q: Finish the serialize and deserialize functions of DurationTransformer. serialize returns the tagged object with the minutes; deserialize reads $value and throws a TypeError unless it is a whole number of at least 0. The program should print the two lines in the comments.
questions.explain: serialize must return the whole { $type, $value } object so the reader knows what it was. deserialize checks the outside data before it builds a Duration.

questions.q: Version 3 of the reminder adds channel. Finish upgrade so version 2 payloads become version 3 with channel: "email", and version 3 payloads are returned as they are. The program should print the two lines in the comments.
questions.explain: A payload that is already current is returned unchanged. An older one gets the new field with the default that matches old behaviour: reminders used to be sent by email. Keep v first so the shape is easy to read.
questions.expected:
{ v: 3, taskId: 2, userId: 'user-ada', channel: 'email' }
{ v: 3, taskId: 3, userId: 'user-ada', channel: 'push' }

questions.q: Upgrade one version at a time. toV2 is done. Finish upgrade so it accepts version 1, 2 or 3 and always returns version 3, reusing toV2 for version 1 (version 3 adds channel: "email"). The program should print 3 user-ada email twice.
questions.explain: Each step upgrades one version, and the steps chain: 1 becomes 2 with toV2, then 2 becomes 3. Adding version 4 later means one more small step, not rewriting the others.

questions.q: Finish readEnvelope(envelope) with deserializeFromEnvelope(envelope, serializer, "json"). If it throws, return "refused". The program should print true and then refused.
questions.explain: The reader checks the envelope before it reads the data. A version it does not understand is refused with an error instead of being misread, and your code decides what to do with it.

questions.q: For a public API you send plain JSON with dates as ISO strings. Finish parseTask(text): parse the JSON and turn due back into a Date, but return null if due is not a valid date. The program should print true and then null.
questions.explain: An invalid date has NaN as its time, so check Number.isNaN(due.getTime()). In a real API a schema does this conversion and check for you, as in the validation lesson.

questions.q: You must read JSON from outside without the serializer. Finish safeParse(text): use JSON.parse with a reviver function that drops the keys __proto__, constructor and prototype (a reviver drops a key when it returns undefined). The program should print [ 'name' ] undefined.
questions.explain: The reviver sees every key while the object is rebuilt. Returning undefined for the dangerous keys means they never reach your objects. The serializer does this for you; it is good to know why.

questions.q: Write a tiny version of type tagging. Finish tag(obj): return a copy of the object where each Date value becomes { $type: "Date", $value: its ISO string } and each Set becomes { $type: "Set", $value: an array of its items }. Other values stay as they are. The program should print the line in the comment.
questions.explain: Check each value with instanceof and replace it with a tagged object that plain JSON can hold. The real serializer does the same at any depth, for more types, and also reads the tags back.
